marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q001.takeaway: Medial pterygoid forms anteromedial relation of parotid gland.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q001.displayText: The anteromedial surface of the parotid gland is related to the medial pterygoid muscle. The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland. It is usually in the shape of an inverted pyramid and has a superior surface, apex, superficial surface, anteromedial surface, and posteromedial surface. Relations: superior surface - external acoustic meatus and posterior part of temporomandibular joint; apex - posterior belly of digastric and carotid triangle; superficial surface - skin, superficial fascia, greater auricular nerve, parotid lymph nodes, and platysma; anteromedial surface - posteroinferior mandibular ramus, masseter, medial pterygoid, and temporomandibular joint; posteromedial surface - mastoid process, posterior belly of digastric, styloid process, and attached muscles.

rationales.a: Mastoid process is a posterior parotid relation, not the anteromedial muscle asked for.
rationales.c: Superficial parotid lymph nodes lie on the gland rather than forming its anteromedial relation.
rationales.d: Styloid process is posterior/deep to the gland but the medial pterygoid is the anteromedial muscular relation.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q002.takeaway: Parotid lymph nodes lie on superficial surface, not behind gland.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q002.displayText: The parotid nodes lie on the superficial surface of the parotid gland. The false capsule covering the parotid gland is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Structures present in the parotid gland from superficial to deep are the facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery. The parotid gland is derived from ectoderm.
emphasis: The parotid nodes lie on the superficial surface
facial nerve, retromandibular vein, and external carotid artery

rationales.a: Investing deep cervical fascia contributes the false capsule around parotid gland.
rationales.b: Retromandibular vein is one of the structures running within parotid gland.
rationales.c: Parotid gland develops from ectoderm; the false statement is that parotid nodes lie behind it (they are superficial).

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q003.takeaway: Facial artery does not pass within parotid gland; external carotid terminates there.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q003.displayText: The facial artery is not present within the parotid gland. The gland contains the external carotid artery, which terminates as maxillary and superficial temporal arteries, and the transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery. Sometimes the external carotid artery gives the posterior auricular artery within the gland. Veins include maxillary and superficial temporal veins, which unite to form the retromandibular vein. Nerves include the facial nerve and its branches; parotid lymph nodes are also present.
emphasis: facial artery is not present within the parotid gland

rationales.a: External carotid enters parotid and terminates there as maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
rationales.c: Transverse facial artery branches from superficial temporal artery and may traverse the gland.
rationales.d: Retromandibular vein forms within the gland; facial artery does not.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q004.takeaway: Otic ganglion lies medial to mandibular nerve, beneath foramen ovale.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q004.displayText: The secretomotor fibres from the glossopharyngeal nerve relay through the otic ganglion before supplying the parotid gland. The otic ganglion is medial to the mandibular nerve. Relations: superiorly - foramen ovale; laterally - mandibular nerve; medially - tensor veli palatini; posteriorly - middle meningeal artery. The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion below the foramen ovale. Preganglionic fibres originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus and pass through the lesser petrosal nerve, the continuation of the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and relay in the ganglion. Postganglionic fibres pass via communicating branches to the auriculotemporal nerve and supply the parotid gland.

rationales.a: Otic ganglion lies anterior to middle meningeal artery; its stated relations place it below foramen ovale.
rationales.b: Otic ganglion is medial to V3 and lateral to tensor veli palatini, so it is not lateral to that muscle.
rationales.d: Otic ganglion lies below foramen ovale; C is incorrect because it is medial, not lateral, to mandibular nerve.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q006.takeaway: Jacobson tympanic nerve brings glossopharyngeal preganglionic fibers into tympanic plexus before lesser petrosal.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q006.displayText: The image shows the foramen ovale. The lesser petrosal nerve passes through this foramen. It derives preganglionic fibres from the tympanic nerve, also known as Jacobson's nerve. The parasympathetic pathway is: inferior salivatory nucleus → glossopharyngeal nerve (tympanic nerve) → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → foramen ovale → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid gland. The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve also passes through the foramen ovale, but it does not have parasympathetic preganglionic fibres.

rationales.b: Cochlear nerve is sensory for hearing and does not carry parasympathetic preganglionic output to otic ganglion.
rationales.c: Nervus intermedius carries facial sensory/parasympathetic fibers, not Jacobson’s IX pathway.
rationales.d: Chorda tympani carries facial parasympathetics to submandibular ganglion; the marked lesser petrosal route derives from Jacobson nerve.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q007.takeaway: Greater petrosal carries parasympathetic route for lacrimal/palatine glands rather than parotid.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q007.displayText: The case is suggestive of parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands, causing increased salivary secretion. Parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland are carried by the lesser petrosal nerve. Preganglionic fibres originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus, travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve and tympanic plexus into the lesser petrosal nerve, and relay in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibres travel through communicating branches to the auriculotemporal nerve and supply the parotid gland. The greater petrosal nerve carries secretomotor fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion and supplies lacrimal, nasal, and palatine glands. Sympathetic supply to the parotid comes from the plexus around the middle meningeal artery. Sensory supply to the gland is via the auriculotemporal nerve, and to the capsule via the greater auricular nerve.

rationales.a: Otic ganglion is the relay for parotid secretion, not the preganglionic nerve carrying salivary parasympathetics in this case.
rationales.c: Auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic fibers from otic ganglion to parotid.
rationales.d: Tympanic plexus is upstream; the named nerve carrying fibers from plexus toward otic ganglion is lesser petrosal, whereas greater petrosal is lacrimal/palatine route.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q008.takeaway: Stensen duct opens opposite second maxillary molar.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q008.displayText: The parotid duct or Stensen's duct opens opposite the 2nd upper molar tooth. It pierces the buccinator at the level of the 3rd upper molar tooth. Structures pierced by the parotid duct are buccal pad of fat, buccopharyngeal fascia, buccinator muscle, and mucous membrane. Clinically, sialolithiasis is more common in the submandibular gland than the parotid. Parotid duct stones are usually radiolucent and rarely visible on plain radiography; contrast is given during sialography to visualize stones.

rationales.a: The duct opens at the second upper molar, not the first.
rationales.c: The parotid duct opens into upper buccal vestibule, not opposite a lower molar.
rationales.d: The opening landmark is second upper molar rather than the second lower molar.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q009.takeaway: Accessory parotid tissue lies between duct and zygomatic arch.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q009.displayText: The accessory parotid gland is present between the parotid duct and zygomatic arch. It is usually a detached part of the parotid gland, with its own blood supply and a secondary duct draining into the main parotid duct. It can be missed during complete parotidectomy, can present as mid-cheek masses, and its histological characteristics can differ from the main gland, so tumors may show a different clinical course.
emphasis: between the parotid duct and zygomatic arch

rationales.a: The accessory gland is not between duct and mandible; its characteristic position is along duct under zygomatic arch.
rationales.b: It is not simply below the parotid apex; accessory tissue may lie in cheek separate from main gland.
rationales.c: The accessory parotid gland is between duct and zygomatic arch, not above the arch.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q010.takeaway: Auriculotemporal nerve carries aberrantly redirected postganglionic parotid fibers in Frey syndrome.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q010.displayText: Frey's syndrome occurs due to aberrant innervation of the auriculotemporal nerve and is also known as gustatory sweating or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery or trauma with injury to the parotid capsule. During regrowth, an aberrant connection develops between parasympathetic fibres supplying the parotid gland (auriculotemporal nerve) and sweat glands. This causes sweating, warmth, and redness of the face during salivary stimulation by smell or taste of food. Management includes antiperspirants (aluminum chloride), tympanic neurectomy, and botulinum toxin injection into affected skin.

rationales.a: Frey syndrome is linked to auriculotemporal parasympathetic fibers, not the facial motor nerve.
rationales.b: Glossopharyngeal is the preganglionic source, but aberrant postganglionic regrowth to sweat glands is via auriculotemporal nerve.
rationales.d: Great auricular is a cervical cutaneous nerve, not the parotid secretomotor pathway.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q011.takeaway: Mylohyoid separates superficial and deep portions of submandibular gland.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q011.displayText: The structure marked X is the submandibular gland. Lobes of the submandibular gland are divided by the mylohyoid muscle. The gland has a larger superficial and smaller deep part separated by mylohyoid; they are continuous around the posterior border of mylohyoid.
emphasis: larger superficial and smaller deep part

rationales.b: Genioglossus forms tongue bulk and does not divide submandibular gland lobes.
rationales.c: Stylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle, not the structure separating gland portions.
rationales.d: Styloglossus moves tongue; mylohyoid separates superficial/deep gland parts.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q012.takeaway: Lingual nerve crosses submandibular duct and is vulnerable during gland removal.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q012.displayText: The lingual nerve is susceptible to injury during excision of the submandibular gland. It loops around the submandibular duct and is therefore vulnerable during procedures in this region. Superficial to hyoglossus, the submandibular duct lies between lingual and hypoglossal nerves. As the duct reaches the anterior border of hyoglossus, it is crossed by the lingual nerve.

rationales.a: Mandibular nerve is proximal V3 trunk; the nerve crossing the duct is its lingual branch.
rationales.c: Inferior alveolar nerve enters mandibular foramen and does not loop around submandibular duct.
rationales.d: Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies larynx and is not at risk in submandibular duct dissection.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q013.takeaway: Submandibular gland wraps around posterior edge of mylohyoid; facial artery relates to superficial part.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q013.displayText: The swelling is in the submandibular region and involves the submandibular gland. The gland wraps around the posterior border of the mylohyoid. It has larger superficial and smaller deep parts continuous around this posterior border. The facial artery is related to the superficial part of the gland. The lingual nerve loops around the submandibular duct, and damage to it causes loss of sensation in the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue.
emphasis: The gland wraps around the posterior border of the mylohyoid

rationales.b: Facial artery is related to the superficial part of the submandibular gland, not the deep part.
rationales.c: Lingual nerve loops around the duct; it is not the hypoglossal nerve that loops beneath it.
rationales.d: Lingual nerve carries general sensation/taste from anterior two-thirds, not posterior third, which is glossopharyngeal territory.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q014.takeaway: Superior salivatory nucleus provides preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to submandibular ganglion.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q014.displayText: Preganglionic fibres to the submandibular ganglion arise from the superior salivatory nucleus. The secretomotor pathway is superior salivatory nucleus → facial nerve → chorda tympani → lingual nerve → submandibular ganglion (relay) → postganglionic fibres → submandibular and sublingual glands.

rationales.b: Inferior salivatory nucleus sends fibers through CN IX to otic ganglion and parotid gland.
rationales.c: Nucleus of tractus solitarius receives visceral/taste afferents; it is not the preganglionic secretomotor source.
rationales.d: Nucleus ambiguus supplies branchial motor fibers, not submandibular parasympathetic outflow.
